lead.t: All of the following are features of multiple myeloma, except:
lead.s: Internal Medicine (MBIM 4100) main exam, Paper One: 3 July 2019

b: The most common variant. Approximately 20,000 new cases per year in the United States. Median age at diagnosis is 70 years; more common in males and in people of African origin. Principally involves bone marrow with lytic lesions throughout
Free light chains only (κ or λ) — 15–20%; excreted in urine as Bence Jones proteins
Most malignant plasma cells secrete both complete immunoglobulins and free light chains → both M proteins and Bence Jones proteins
Chromosomal translocations involving the IgH locus (chromosome 14) and various partners including cyclin D1, FGFR3, and cyclin D3 → dysregulation of D cyclins is common
Late in course, MYC translocations may also occur

qs.q: Which baseline laboratory investigation is specifically useful to help rule out multiple myeloma when evaluating a patient with osteoporosis?
qs.e: Serum protein electrophoresis is indicated because multiple myeloma may be associated with secondary osteoporosis. Thyroid-stimulating hormone evaluates thyroid dysfunction, not multiple myeloma.

qs.q: Which cell type predominantly proliferates in the bone marrow in multiple myeloma?
qs.e: Multiple myeloma is a malignant B cell disorder characterized by the predominance of plasma cells in the marrow. T lymphocytes are not the primary proliferating malignant cell line in this condition.

qs.q: What is the typical ratio of male to female incidence in multiple myeloma?
qs.e: Epidemiological data shows that multiple myeloma affects males to females in a 2:1 ratio. An equal 1:1 ratio does not reflect the documented disease demographics.

qs.q: A patient presents with smoldering multiple myeloma. Which of the following findings characterizes this intermediate condition?
o: M protein level of 3g/dl or more
qs.e: Smoldering multiple myeloma is characterized by an M protein level of 3g/dl or more and greater than 10 percent clonal plasma cells without end-organ damage. End-organ damage distinguishes symptomatic myeloma from the smoldering phase.

qs.q: Which peripheral blood film finding is classically associated with multiple myeloma due to abnormal protein levels?
qs.e: Rouleaux formation on a peripheral blood film is caused by high levels of circulating paraprotein altering red blood cell suspension. Schistocytes are indicative of microangiopathic hemolytic anemias rather than standard myeloma presentations.

qs.q: Which radiological feature is classically seen on X-rays of patients with multiple myeloma?
qs.e: Multiple myeloma X-rays characteristically display multiple punched out lytic lesions with a lack of reactive bone formation. Sclerotic lesions are more typical of other malignancies like prostate cancer.

qs.q: Which immunohistochemical marker is characteristically positive in multiple myeloma plasma cells?
qs.e: Wait, let me review the note: Immunohistochemistry is positive for CD56. CD20 is a pan-B cell marker, but plasma cells aberrantly express CD56 in myeloma. Let me make sure CD56 is the correct option chosen as correct.

qs.q: Which of the following represents part of the classic diagnostic triad for multiple myeloma?
qs.e: The classic triad includes marrow plasmacytosis greater than 10 percent, lytic bone lesions, and serum or urine M component. Serum alkaline phosphatase is typically normal in multiple myeloma.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma‑cell disorder that produces excess monoclonal immunoglobulin or free light chains, causing bone destruction, anemia, renal injury and immune suppression.

sections.p: Clonal proliferation of plasma cells in bone marrow that meets ≥10% plasma cells or a biopsy‑proven plasmacytoma plus evidence of organ damage (CRAB).
b: ≥10% clonal plasma cells on marrow or biopsy‑proven plasmacytoma
Monoclonal protein in serum or urine (M‑protein)
CRAB: hyperCalcaemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions

t.b: Detects and types the M‑protein; a sharp spike confirms monoclonal gammopathy
Quantifies κ/λ ratio; abnormal ratio supports diagnosis, especially when M‑protein is low
Counts plasma cells and assesses cytogenetics; ≥10% confirms disease

t.a: Skeletal survey or low‑dose whole‑body CT
t.b: Shows lytic lesions or osteoporosis; needed for the ‘B’ of CRAB
Identifies organ damage; hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anemia are red flags

sections.p: The International Staging System (ISS) uses serum β2‑microglobulin and albumin to stratify risk; cytogenetics add a revised ISS (R‑ISS).
b: ISS II: intermediate values

t.b: Low albumin (<4 g/dL) worsens stage; reflects nutrition and disease activity
Detects high‑risk cytogenetic lesions; guides therapy intensity

sections.p: Most cases are sporadic; risk factors include age, male sex, African ancestry, and prior exposure to radiation or certain chemicals.
b: Age > 60 years (median 70)
Male gender, African descent
Prior radiation or occupational benzene exposure

sections.p: Patients often have persistent back or bone pain, fatigue, recurrent infections, and signs of anemia or renal dysfunction.
b: Dull back pain, worsened by movement
Unexplained anemia → fatigue, pallor
Renal insufficiency: polyuria, edema

sections.p: Combine laboratory, imaging and marrow studies to confirm diagnosis, stage disease and assess organ damage.
b: Serum/urine electrophoresis, free light‑chain assay
Complete blood count, calcium, creatinine, albumin
Whole‑body low‑dose CT or MRI for bone lesions

t.b: Detects Bence Jones protein; positive result supports light‑chain disease
Identifies occult vertebral lesions not seen on X‑ray
Provides some cytogenetic information; less sensitive but better than none

sections.p: Complications drive urgency: hypercalcaemia, renal failure, pathological fractures, and infection.
b: Serum calcium >11 mg/dL → cardiac arrhythmia risk
Creatinine rise >2 mg/dL → dialysis may be needed
Spinal compression fracture → neurologic deficit

sections.p: Treat the clone with anti‑myeloma therapy, protect kidneys, control calcium and prevent infections.
b: Proteasome inhibitors (e.g., bortezomib) – disrupt plasma‑cell protein handling
Immunomodulatory drugs (lenalidomide, pomalidomide) – enhance immune clearance
Steroids (dexamethasone) – rapid tumour reduction, anti‑inflammatory
Bisphosphonates or denosumab – inhibit osteoclast‑mediated bone loss
Autologous stem‑cell transplant for eligible patients

sections.p: Regular monitoring for disease progression, treatment toxicity and secondary malignancies.
b: Every 2–3 months: CBC, calcium, creatinine, M‑protein level
Annual skeletal imaging if symptoms change
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce infection risk

sections.p: Conditions that also cause bone pain, anemia and monoclonal proteins.
b: Metastatic bone disease – usually multiple solid‑tumour sources, not plasma‑cell clone
Waldenström macroglobulinemia – IgM monoclonal protein, hyperviscosity rather than lytic lesions
AL amyloidosis – light‑chain deposition without overt bone disease

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal early in disease.
b: Serum electrophoresis can miss low‑level light‑chain disease; add free‑light‑chain assay
Normal calcium does not exclude early bone loss; imaging is essential
Renal function may appear normal until late; monitor urine protein

whenToSeekHelp: Severe bone pain with fever (possible fracture or infection)
Rapid decline in urine output or creatinine >2 mg/dL

faq.q: Why is the free light‑chain ratio important?
faq.a: It detects light‑chain disease when the M‑spike is small and predicts renal risk.
It is treatable and can achieve long remission, but most patients eventually relapse.

faq.q: What causes the anemia in myeloma?
faq.a: Bone‑marrow infiltration reduces red‑cell production and chronic disease inflammation suppresses erythropoiesis.
